title: Mental health in people with a learning disability
blurb: Recognise how mental health problems present differently in people with a learning disability and apply NICE NG54 to assessment and treatment.
question: Marcus, 31, has a moderate learning disability. Since his grandmother died three months ago he has stopped going to his day service, needs more prompting to wash, and sleeps much more. Staff say he is 'being lazy'. How should the nurse assess and support him?

teach.body: People with a learning disability are at increased risk of mental health problems. They develop them for the same reasons as anyone (bereavement, money worries, relationship problems), but problems may present differently, usual symptoms may not be reported or observable, and they are commonly overlooked. In plain English: low mood or anxiety may look like a change in behaviour, lost skills or withdrawal rather than a description of feelings.

teach.h: Behaviour changes that should prompt a mental health check
head: Change
Example
rows: Needs prompting to wash or dress
teach.caption: NICE NG54 1.6.1: consider a mental health problem if any of these appear.

teach.body: If a mental health problem is suspected, triage it: describe the nature, severity and duration and agree an action plan (NG54 1.6.4). Refer suspected serious mental illness or dementia to a psychiatrist with expertise in learning disabilities (1.6.5). Assessment should be in a familiar place where possible, with people who know the person; be aware that a physical condition may cause or mask the problem (1.7.1-1.7.2), and use carers' information about recent change (1.7.5).

head: Tool
Use
teach.caption: NG11 1.5.11 names PAS-ADD and DASH-II for screening when a mental health problem may underlie behaviour; NG54 1.7.10-1.7.12 name the others.

teach.body: Some genetic conditions bring particular mental health risks, and NICE NG54 asks assessors to look for them so they can be treated: for example anxiety in autistic people and psychosis in people with Prader-Willi syndrome. Adults with Down syndrome should have a baseline assessment of adaptive behaviour so later decline, which may signal dementia, can be measured (NG54 1.7.13).

teach.caption: NG54 1.8.5-1.8.7 and 1.9.2-1.9.8. Avoid sub-therapeutic doses as well as excessive ones.

teach.body: Marcus, 31, has withdrawn, needs prompting with washing and is sleeping more since his grandmother died. The nurse treats this as a possible mental health problem, not laziness. She arranges a GP review for physical causes (thyroid, pain, medicines), triages his mood using information from staff and his mother, and refers to the community learning disability team. A Glasgow Depression Scale helps track change. He is offered adapted bereavement support and adapted CBT.

teach.text: Diagnostic overshadowing works for mental health too: 'that's just his learning disability' or 'he's being lazy' can hide depression. And under the Mental Health Act 1983 (current law), a learning disability counts as a mental disorder for longer-term detention under s3 only if it is associated with 'abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct' (s1(2A)-(2B)), and the other s3 criteria must still be met; the 2025 Act's further changes are coming but not yet in force.

items: Higher risk, different presentation, often overlooked (NG54 1.2.8).
Consider mental illness when skills are lost or behaviour changes (NG54 1.6.1).
Exclude physical causes; use carers' knowledge; triage then refer to LD psychiatry if serious.
Adapted CBT for depression in milder LD; relaxation and graded exposure for anxiety.
Medicines: specialist start in more severe LD, lowest effective dose, one change at a time.

summary: You can now recognise how mental health problems may present in people with a learning disability, exclude physical causes, triage and refer appropriately, and apply NICE NG54 to adapted psychological and medication treatment.

A.q: According to NICE NG54, which change in a person with a learning disability should prompt staff to consider a mental health problem?
options: A request to change day service
Needing more prompting to use skills
Asking to see a family member more
Choosing a new activity at college
A.why: NG54 1.6.1 lists loss of skills or needing more prompting, social withdrawal, irritability, avoidance, agitation and loss of interest as changes that should prompt consideration of a mental health problem.

whyNot.0: A request to change service is a choice, not a listed warning sign.
whyNot.2: Wanting more family contact is not a listed sign.
whyNot.3: Choosing a new activity suggests interest, not loss of it.

A.q: NICE NG54 recommends considering which psychological therapy for depression in people with milder learning disabilities?
options: Long-term psychodynamic psychotherapy
Eye movement desensitisation therapy
Adapted cognitive behavioural therapy
Dialectical behaviour therapy group
A.why: NG54 1.8.5: consider CBT adapted for people with learning disabilities to treat depression or subthreshold depressive symptoms in milder learning disabilities.

whyNot.0: Psychodynamic therapy is not the recommendation in NG54.
whyNot.1: EMDR is not recommended in NG54 for depression.
whyNot.3: DBT is not the NG54 recommendation for depression.

A.q: Which tool does NICE NG54 suggest for monitoring depressive symptoms over time in adults with a learning disability?
options: The Glasgow Depression Scale
The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale
The Abbey Pain Scale
The Mini Mental State Examination
A.why: NG54 1.7.11: consider a formal measure such as the Glasgow Depression Scale, self-report for milder learning disabilities or the carer supplement for any degree.

whyNot.1: The EPDS is designed for perinatal depression.
whyNot.2: The Abbey scale assesses pain in people who cannot report it.
whyNot.3: The MMSE is a cognitive screen, not a depression measure.

B.q: Hana, 29, has a moderate learning disability. Over six weeks she has become irritable and stopped eating breakfast. Before referring for a mental health assessment, what should the nurse do first?
options: Start an ABC chart for the irritability
Ask the GP to start an antidepressant
Arrange checks for physical causes
Refer her to a talking therapy service
B.why: NG54 1.7.2: an underlying physical health condition may be causing the problem or masking a mental health problem, so physical causes such as pain, reflux, thyroid disease or medicine effects must be checked.

whyNot.0: Recording behaviour may help, but physical causes must be excluded first.
whyNot.1: Starting medication before assessment is premature.
whyNot.3: Referral may follow, but a physical cause has not been excluded.

B.q: Ian, 42, has Prader-Willi syndrome. His carers report that he has started talking to people who are not there. Why is NICE NG54 particularly relevant?
options: It says this is part of his syndrome and not treatable
It names psychosis as a phenotype-linked risk to assess
It says hearing voices is normal in learning disability
It says no assessment is needed if he is calm
B.why: NG54 1.7.4 asks assessors to look for problems associated with behavioural phenotypes, giving psychosis in Prader-Willi syndrome as an example, so that they can be treated.

whyNot.0: NG54 says phenotype-linked problems should be assessed so they can be treated.
whyNot.2: Hallucinations are not a normal feature of learning disability.
whyNot.3: Calmness does not remove the need to assess a possible psychosis.

B.q: Ola, 38, has a severe learning disability and suspected depression. Who should start antidepressant medication, according to NICE NG54?
options: Her GP at the next annual health check
A pharmacist under a patient group direction
Her community learning disability nurse
A specialist with expertise in LD mental health
B.why: NG54 1.9.2: only specialists with expertise in mental health in learning disabilities should start medication for adults with more severe learning disabilities, unless locally agreed shared-care protocols exist.

whyNot.0: The GP is not the recommended initiator for more severe learning disabilities.
whyNot.1: A PGD is not the route for starting long-term psychotropic treatment.
whyNot.2: The nurse has a key role in monitoring but the recommendation is for specialist initiation.

C.q: Marcus, 31, has a moderate learning disability. Since his grandmother died three months ago he has withdrawn from his day service, needs prompting to wash and sleeps more. His thyroid tests and medicines review are normal. Staff call him 'lazy'. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Agree a reward plan to motivate him back to day service
Triage for depression and refer to the community LD team
Wait another three months as grief takes time to settle
Ask the GP to prescribe a sleeping tablet for his routine
C.why: His changes match NG54 1.6.1 warning signs and physical causes are excluded. Triage (nature, severity, duration) and referral for assessment are next; labelling him 'lazy' is overshadowing.

whyNot.0: A reward plan treats a possible depression as a motivation problem.
whyNot.2: Waiting risks a treatable illness worsening; grief and depression can coexist.
whyNot.3: Sleeping more is a symptom to assess, not a reason for hypnotics.

C.q: Dev, 26, has a learning disability and takes an antipsychotic started years ago for behaviour that challenges. He has no psychotic symptoms. What does NICE NG54 recommend?
options: Continue unchanged because he is settled
Switch to a different antipsychotic
Consider reducing or stopping it
Add a second drug to lower the dose
C.why: NG54 1.9.7: for people taking antipsychotics without psychotic symptoms, consider reducing or discontinuing, review afterwards, and document annually the reasons if it is continued. This also reflects STOMP.

whyNot.0: Long-term continuation without review is what NG54 and STOMP aim to change.
whyNot.1: Switching does not address whether he needs an antipsychotic.
whyNot.3: Adding drugs increases polypharmacy; NG54 advises changing one drug at a time.

C.q: Ruby, 33, has a mild learning disability and a fear of dogs that stops her going out. Which intervention does NICE NG54 recommend considering?
options: A short course of a benzodiazepine before trips
Avoiding routes where dogs are likely to be
An antipsychotic at the lowest effective dose
Graded exposure, supported by her carers
C.why: NG54 1.8.7: consider graded exposure techniques for anxiety symptoms or phobias, with support to practise between sessions (1.8.4).

whyNot.0: Benzodiazepines are not the NG54 recommendation for phobia.
whyNot.1: Avoidance maintains the phobia and narrows her life.
whyNot.2: Antipsychotics are not indicated for a specific phobia.

reteach.title: Same illnesses, different signals
reteach.question: If someone cannot say 'I feel low', how might depression show itself?

blocks.body: People with a learning disability get the same mental illnesses as everyone else, but may show them through what they do rather than what they say: stopping activities, losing skills, needing more prompting, sleeping or eating differently, irritability. Carers who know the person are the best detectors of change.

blocks.text: 'Lazy', 'stubborn' or 'attention-seeking' are red-flag labels. Ask what has changed and why.

explain.body: Higher risk; may present differently; symptoms may not be reported; commonly overlooked (NG54 1.2.8).

test.q: Which statement about mental health problems in people with a learning disability is correct?
options: They are less common than in the general population
They present in exactly the same way as in others
They are caused by the learning disability itself
They are often overlooked or attributed to the disability
test.why: NG54 says mental health problems are commonly overlooked and may present differently.

whyNot.1: Presentation may differ, especially in more severe LD.
whyNot.2: They arise for the same reasons as in anyone, such as bereavement.

explain.body: NG54 1.6.4: triage nature, severity and duration with an action plan. 1.6.5: refer suspected serious mental illness or dementia to a psychiatrist with LD expertise.

test.q: A man with a learning disability shows signs of a possible psychosis. Where should he be referred according to NICE NG54?
options: A psychiatrist with expertise in learning disabilities
His GP at his next routine annual health check
A general adult talking therapy service nearby
A neurologist for an urgent brain MRI scan
test.why: NG54 1.6.5: refer suspected serious mental illness or dementia to a psychiatrist with expertise in mental health problems in learning disabilities.

whyNot.1: A routine annual check is too slow for suspected psychosis.
whyNot.2: Talking therapy services are not the route for suspected psychosis.
whyNot.3: Neurology is not the first referral for psychosis.

explain.body: A physical condition may cause or mask a mental health problem (NG54 1.7.2). Check pain, thyroid, infection, constipation and medicine effects.

test.q: A woman with Down syndrome becomes slow and withdrawn. Which physical cause is particularly important to check?
options: Hypothyroidism
Iron overload
Vitamin C deficiency
High blood pressure
test.why: Hypothyroidism is common in Down syndrome and can mimic depression or dementia.

whyNot.1: Iron overload is not a typical cause of this picture.
whyNot.2: Vitamin C deficiency is not the key check here.
whyNot.3: Hypertension does not usually present this way.

explain.body: Specialist start in more severe LD (1.9.2); lowest effective dose, avoid sub-therapeutic doses (1.9.5); antipsychotics without psychosis: consider reducing (1.9.7); one change at a time (1.9.8).

test.q: When switching psychotropic medicines in a person with a learning disability, what does NICE NG54 advise?
options: Change two drugs together to save time
Stop the first drug abruptly then start
Change one drug at a time
Use the maximum dose of the new drug
test.why: NG54 1.9.8: change one drug at a time so discontinuation or interaction effects can be identified.

whyNot.0: Changing two at once makes effects impossible to attribute.
whyNot.3: NG54 advises the lowest effective dose.
